edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina 5 (1844), via Latin Wikisource
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Militiae nomen cum dederis, freno teneris. Incipe tunc ergo dimittere pristina gesta: Luxurias vita, quoniam labor imminet armis. Imperio regis omni virtute parendum, Tempora postrema si vis pertingere laeta. Ille bonus miles, semper exspecta fruenda; Blandire noli tibi, desidias omnino mitte, Ut tuo praeposito cottidie praesto sis, ante Solicitus esto, matutinus signa revise. Cum videris bellum, agonia sume propinqua. Haec gloria regis, militem videre paratum; Rex adest, optato propter spem dominicaturum. Ille parat dona, ille pro victoria laetus Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse. Tu tibi praeterea in Belian parcere noli: Impiger esto magis, ut reddat famam pro morte.
pass_a_gloss: When you have given the name of soldier, you are held by a bridle. Begin then to dismiss former deeds: a life of luxury, because labor with arms is imminent. To the command of the king, obedience is to be given with all virtue, if you wish to reach the last times joyful. He, a good soldier, always expects things to be enjoyed; do not flatter yourself, completely send away idleness, so that you may be present daily to your commander, be solicitous beforehand, revise the signals in the morning. When you see war, take up nearby agony. This is the glory of the king, to see the soldier prepared; the king is present, who will dominate because of the hoped-for hope. He prepares gifts, he, joyful for victory, receives, and designates his own attendant to be. You, moreover, do not spare yourself in respect to Belial: be more energetic, so that he may give fame in exchange for death.

pass_b_english: Once you take the name of soldier, you are bridled. So put your old life behind you: discard luxury, because hard labor under arms lies ahead. Obey the King’s command with every virtue, if you want to reach the final days in joy. A good soldier always looks for the reward; do not coddle yourself, cast off all laziness, so that you report to your commander each day—be ready beforehand, check the signals at dawn. When you see battle coming, take up the agony at hand. The King’s glory is to see his soldier prepared; the King is here, and he will reign because of the hope we wait for. He readies gifts, he welcomes victory with joy, and he appoints his own attendant. As for you, do not spare yourself against Belial: be all the more vigorous, so that he may give you renown in exchange for death.

review.notes: Pass B introduces a subject not present in the Latin source: 'because of the hope we wait for' for 'propter spem dominicaturum'. The Latin 'spem' (hope) is the object of the preposition, but the addition of 'we wait for' is an interpretive expansion not found in the text. Additionally, Pass A's translation of 'Suscipit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse' as 'receives, and designates his own attendant to be' is grammatically awkward and fails to capture the sense of the infinitive 'esse' as part of the designation/appointment, though Pass B is more fluent, it fails the fidelity check by adding 'we wait for'.
reasons: Pass B adds 'we wait for' to 'propter spem dominicaturum', which is not in the source text.
